items.output:
Snow fell in soft sheets, blanketing the forest until every branch wore a white sleeve. Inside the cabin, I stirred a pot of mulled cider, steam fogging the windows that framed the world in silver. I had come alone for the weekend, seeking stillness, and I was getting it: no buzzing phones, no deadlines, just the low thud of skis on packed drifts outside and the occasional crackle of pine logs in the stove.

On Saturday I laced up my boots and followed a trail I had broken with my own steps, each kick a punctuation mark in the silence. I paused at a rise, breath rising like smoke, and looked down at the valley below, where the sun was just beginning to spill gold across the ice of a frozen lake. I stayed until my fingers throbbed, then turned back, following my own tracks in reverse, a quiet loop I could never quite retrace exactly.

That night I read by candlelight, pages trembling in the draft from the sill. When I finally climbed into the loft, I left the curtains open so I could watch the moon glaze the snow with light. I slept with the window ajar, letting in the cold that smelled of pine and smoke, and I dreamed of nothing at all.

More soon.

items.output: Learning to swim as an adult was both terrifying and exhilarating. I made my way to the pool with a mix of anxiety and determination, stepping into the water with hesitant feet. The water was colder than I expected, and I made slow, cautious movements, trying to keep my balance. I remember the instructor encouraging me with a calm voice, guiding me through each stroke with patience. It took time, but I began to feel more confident with every lap I completed. Now, I swim with ease, grateful for the day I decided to face my fear.

# Learning to Swim as an Adult

The water was cold and I was older than most kids in the class. I stepped in up to my ankles and paused. The instructor waved me forward. I moved one step deeper. I took a breath and dunked my face. I opened my eyes under the surface. I saw nothing but ripples. I came up coughing. I tried again. I put my face in and blew bubbles. I watched them rise and vanish. I reached for the wall with my arms. I pushed off and kicked. I moved an inch. I did it again. I moved a foot. I laughed under my breath. I looked at the instructor and gave a thumbs up. I was swimming. I was moving through water with my own power. I was not sinking. I was not afraid. I was free.
